full_texts.text:
Inflation in Taiwan is no longer a background statistic. With CPI and PPI both running hot, costs are pressing into every aisle of the supermarket and every refrigerated truck on the highway, which can either squeeze profits or reward businesses that handle pricing power well. This article walks through three Taiwan Food & Grocery Retail and Cold-Chain Logistics Beneficiaries stocks exposed to these trends, and why their stories may belong on your watchlist today.
The three Taiwan Food & Grocery Retail and Cold-Chain Logistics Beneficiaries stocks below are only a starting sample, and the full idea screen surfaced 0 more companies with equally compelling narratives that are not covered in this article.
Overview: Uni-President Enterprises is a large Taiwanese food and beverage group supplying instant noodles, drinks, and packaged foods across Asian grocery channels.
Market Cap: NT$436.4b
Uni-President Enterprises fits into the screener theme as a scale player that helps stock Taiwanese shelves with branded noodles, drinks, and frozen foods, while also running its own logistics and distribution services. That reach gives the group meaningful room to adjust prices as CPI and PPI remain elevated. However, grocery investors may still monitor what happens if one unseen pressure on input costs and pricing power changes.
If you want to see how that pressure shows up in the numbers, go straight to the analysis report for Uni-President Enterprises to see the pricing power and cost risks clearly presented.
Overview: Charoen Pokphand Enterprise (Taiwan) produces animal feed, breeds poultry and livestock, and processes meat and food products for Taiwan's supply chain.
Operations: The group generates roughly NT$13.8b from feed, NT$7.4b from meat processing, NT$6.2b from food processing, primarily across Taiwan.
Market Cap: NT$30.7b
Charoen Pokphand Enterprise (Taiwan) sits closer to the farm and factory than the checkout line. It feeds Taiwan's supermarkets through NT$29.7b in local revenue while PPI and food costs keep rising. Investors watching its P/E discount and high dividend may focus less on that headline yield and more on what happens if one unseen pressure on cash generation persists.
Overview: President Chain Store runs Taiwan’s 7-Eleven and related grocery, supermarket, and logistics formats, linking everyday staples to nationwide convenience spending.
Operations: President Chain Store earns most revenue from convenience stores of about NT$226.5b, plus NT$115.3b from distribution and NT$23.9b from logistics.
Market Cap: NT$218.8b
President Chain Store gives you direct exposure to Taiwan’s inflation resilient 7-Eleven ecosystem. Essential groceries, convenience services, and logistics infrastructure combine with steady foot traffic and pricing power. Recent CPI and PPI data suggest that small shifts in how far customers absorb higher shelf and energy costs could matter a lot if one unseen pressure on spending habits changes.
If those spending shifts are what interest you, go straight to the 3 key rewards and 1 important warning sign to see whether President Chain Store’s resilience is masking something bigger.

full_texts.title: US cites China in PNG closure of Taiwan site - Taipei Times
full_texts.text:
The US government has expressed concern over the closure of Taiwan’s representative office in Papua New Guinea (PNG) under pressure from the PNG government, saying that the incident is another example of Beijing’s intimidation of Taiwan.
“We are deeply concerned by reports that the government of Papua New Guinea has unilaterally ordered the closure of the Taipei Economic Office in Port Moresby,” an unnamed US Department of State spokesman said on Saturday.
“Taiwan is a reliable, like-minded and democratic partner, and its relationships around the world provide significant benefits to the citizens of those countries, including Papua New Guinea,” the spokesman said.
Photo: Reuters
“This is yet another example of Beijing’s intimidation campaign against Taiwan and its supporters around the world, which undermines the sovereign decisions of countries choosing to partner with Taiwan and threatens international peace and prosperity,” the spokesman added.
The US Department of State made the remarks in response to a request for comment on Taiwan’s decision on Friday to close its representative office in PNG, which was established in 1990 despite the absence of official diplomatic ties.
The decision came after the PNG government renewed its unilateral demands that personnel of the Taipei Economic Office in Port Moresby leave the country and that the office be shut down, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) said.
“In consideration of national dignity, diplomatic autonomy and overall national interests, and following a comprehensive assessment, the ROC [Taiwan] government has made the decision to close the office, withdraw all stationed personnel, and conduct a full review and adjustment of bilateral ties,” the ministry said in a statement issued on Friday.
The dispute began after PNG Minister of Foreign Affairs Justin Tkatchenko announced on July 16 that his government had ordered the immediate closure of Taiwan’s representative office in the country, citing PNG’s adherence to the “one China” policy.
Taiwan promptly lodged a formal protest with the PNG government, but maintained that its representative office remained operational despite the unilateral announcement.
Taiwan also suspended spot purchases of liquefied natural gas from PNG in July in response to the country’s plans to close Taiwan’s representative office.
China has long used political coercion, economic incentives and diplomatic pressure to force other countries to accept its political claims, while seeking to limit Taiwan’s international presence, MOFA said.
The PNG government’s decision is another example of Beijing using political and economic leverage to interfere in other countries’ diplomatic decisions, undermining international trust and fairness, it said, urging the international community to recognize China’s efforts to isolate Taiwan on the global stage.

full_texts.title: My Take | Taiwan doth complain too much about Beijing - South China Morning Post
full_texts.text:
Taiwan doth complain too much about Beijing
Despite being invited to join the Apec leaders’ summit in Shenzhen, Taipei says the mainland has breached protocol
Give Taiwanese president William Lai Ching-te and his Democratic Progressive Party-led government an inch and they’ll take a mile. For more than a year, they demanded to take part as an “equal” in the Apec leaders’ summit in Shenzhen later this month. Now they have been invited. Yet they complain that the invitation is not polite enough and breaches diplomatic protocol.
“Whenever they breach the established rules or diplomatic conventions, we will certainly lodge a protest at the earliest opportunity,” Taiwanese foreign minister Lin Chia-lung told reporters.
What protocol? The island is not a nation; it is part of China. How can Beijing break protocol in whatever way it sees fit to communicate with one of its provinces?
